jp: 祖父[そふ]は{めったに|av-mettani}怒[おこ]らない。
en: My grandfather hardly ever gets angry.
why: めったに + a negative verb means 'rarely': the event happens very seldom.

jp: 東京[とうきょう]では{めったに|av-mettani}雪[ゆき]が降[ふ]りません。
en: It hardly ever snows in Tokyo.
why: Seldom-happening events take めったに + a negative verb.

jp: この店[みせ]にはお客[きゃく]さんが{めったに|av-mettani}来[き]ません。
en: Customers hardly ever come to this shop.
why: A very low frequency with a negative verb is めったに ('rarely').

jp: 父[ちち]は家[いえ]で{めったに|av-mettani}お酒[さけ]を飲[の]まない。
en: My father rarely drinks alcohol at home.
why: めったに + ない says the habit almost never happens; the others do not express frequency.

jp: 彼女[かのじょ]は{めったに|av-mettani}笑[わら]わない人[ひと]です。
en: She is a person who rarely laughs.
why: The relative clause describes a seldom-occurring action, so めったに + negative.

jp: 私[わたし]は{めったに|av-mettani}風邪[かぜ]をひかない。
en: I rarely catch a cold.
why: Catching a cold is a repeatable event; its rarity is expressed by めったに + ない.

jp: 駅[えき]の近[ちか]くなのに、電車[でんしゃ]は{めったに|av-mettani}使[つか]いません。
en: Even though I live near the station, I hardly ever take the train.
why: The habit of taking the train is almost non-existent: めったに + negative.

jp: あの二人[ふたり]は{めったに|av-mettani}けんかをしない。
en: Those two rarely quarrel.
why: Quarrelling happens very seldom, which is what めったに + ない states.

jp: 祖母[そぼ]は{めったに|av-mettani}外食[がいしょく]しない。
en: My grandmother rarely eats out.
why: Eating out is a habit that hardly ever occurs, so めったに + negative.

jp: 日曜日[にちようび]は{めったに|av-mettani}早[はや]く起[お]きません。
en: I rarely get up early on Sundays.
why: 'Rarely' for a habit takes めったに; 一切 would mean 'never, not at all'.

jp: 弟[おとうと]は野菜[やさい]をめったに{食[た]べない|av-mettani}。
en: My little brother hardly ever eats vegetables.
why: めったに demands a negative predicate; a positive verb is ungrammatical.

jp: 田中[たなか]さんはめったに{遅[おく]れません|av-mettani}。
en: Mr. Tanaka is hardly ever late.
why: めったに must be closed by a negative form, here ません.

jp: 昨夜[ゆうべ]は{ろくに|av-mettani}寝[ね]ていないので、とても眠[ねむ]い。
en: I hardly slept last night, so I'm very sleepy.
why: ろくに + negative means 'not properly / hardly'; a single night is not a frequency, so めったに fails.

jp: 朝[あさ]から忙[いそが]しくて、{ろくに|av-mettani}食[た]べていない。
en: I've been busy since morning and haven't eaten properly.
why: ろくに + negative says the action was not done adequately; this is about today, not a habit.

jp: 前[まえ]の晩[ばん]に{ろくに|av-mettani}勉強[べんきょう]しなかったので、試験[しけん]に落[お]ちてしまった。
en: I barely studied the night before, so I failed the exam.
why: ろくに + negative means 'not nearly enough' for a one-off effort; a single night is not a frequency, so めったに fails.

jp: あの子[こ]は{ろくに|av-mettani}挨拶[あいさつ]もしない。
en: That child doesn't even greet people properly.
why: ろくに + negative criticises an action not done properly or adequately.

jp: 先生[せんせい]の話[はなし]を{ろくに|av-mettani}聞[き]かずに、問題[もんだい]を解[と]き始[はじ]めた。
en: He started on the problems without properly listening to the teacher.
why: ろくに + negative (here ずに) means not doing something properly; めったに cannot join ずに like this.

jp: 風邪[かぜ]で{ろくに|av-mettani}動[うご]けなかった。
en: I could hardly move because of a cold.
why: ろくに + negative potential means 'could not do it adequately'.

jp: 彼[かれ]は漢字[かんじ]もろくに{書[か]けない|av-mettani}。
en: He can't even write kanji properly.
why: ろくに must be followed by a negative; a positive potential form is ungrammatical.

jp: 朝[あさ]ごはんを{ろくに|av-mettani}食[た]べずに家[いえ]を出[で]た。
en: I left home without eating a proper breakfast.
why: ろくに + negative stresses that the meal was inadequate on this occasion.

jp: 忙[いそが]しくて、母[はは]に{ろくに|av-mettani}電話[でんわ]もしていない。
en: I've been busy and haven't even phoned my mother properly.
why: ろくに + negative complains that something has not been done as it should.

jp: 寝不足[ねぶそく]で、ろくに{考[かんが]えられなかった|av-mettani}。
en: I was short of sleep and could hardly think straight.
why: ろくに requires a negative ending; the positive potential forms do not fit.

jp: 高[たか]い店[みせ]が{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}おいしいとは限[かぎ]らない。
en: Expensive restaurants are not necessarily delicious.
why: 必ずしも ... とは限らない is the partial negation 'not necessarily'.

jp: 努力[どりょく]しても{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}成功[せいこう]するわけではない。
en: Even if you make an effort, you don't necessarily succeed.
why: 'Not always the case' is 必ずしも + わけではない; the other words express frequency or total absence.

jp: 有名[ゆうめい]な大学[だいがく]を出[で]ても、{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}幸[しあわ]せになれるとは限[かぎ]りません。
en: Even graduating from a famous university doesn't necessarily make you happy.
why: The point is that the link is not guaranteed, which is 必ずしも ... とは限りません.

jp: 日本人[にほんじん]が{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}納豆[なっとう]が好[す]きなわけではありません。
en: Japanese people don't necessarily all like natto.
why: Denying a generalisation ('not necessarily') takes 必ずしも ... わけではない.

jp: 値段[ねだん]が安[やす]いからといって、{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}品質[ひんしつ]が悪[わる]いとは言[い]えない。
en: Just because the price is low, you can't necessarily say the quality is bad.
why: Rejecting a hasty conclusion ('not necessarily') uses 必ずしも ... とは言えない.

jp: 本[ほん]をたくさん読[よ]んでも、{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}頭[あたま]がよくなるとは限[かぎ]らない。
en: Reading lots of books doesn't necessarily make you smarter.
why: A result that is not guaranteed is expressed by 必ずしも ... とは限らない.

jp: 先生[せんせい]の言[い]うことが{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}正[ただ]しいとは限[かぎ]りません。
en: What a teacher says is not necessarily correct.
why: 'Not necessarily true' is 必ずしも + とは限らない.

jp: みんなが{必[かなら]ずしも|av-mettani}雨[あめ]の日[ひ]を嫌[いや]がるわけではない。
en: Not everyone necessarily dislikes rainy days.
why: 'Not everyone necessarily' denies a generalisation: 必ずしも ... わけではない.

jp: 高[たか]いものが必[かなら]ずしも良[よ]いものだとは{限[かぎ]りません|av-mettani}。
en: Expensive things are not necessarily good things.
why: 必ずしも pairs with とは限らない (negative), never with a positive 限る.

jp: 忙[いそが]しい人[ひと]が必[かなら]ずしも仕事[しごと]ができる{わけではない|av-mettani}。
en: A busy person is not necessarily good at their job.
why: 必ずしも + わけではない means 'it does not necessarily follow'; わけがない means 'no way'.

jp: 日本[にほん]に住[す]んでいても、必[かなら]ずしも日本語[にほんご]が上手[じょうず]な{わけではない|av-mettani}。
en: Living in Japan doesn't necessarily mean one is good at Japanese.
why: The partial negation 必ずしも ... わけではない fits; the others mean 'impossible' or 'cannot'.

jp: この件[けん]については、私[わたし]は{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}関係[かんけい]ありません。
en: I have absolutely nothing to do with this matter.
why: 一切 + negative means 'not at all, without exception'.

jp: 医者[いしゃ]に止[と]められて、今[いま]はお酒[さけ]を{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}飲[の]みません。
en: My doctor told me to stop, so now I don't drink any alcohol at all.
why: A complete ban means 'none at all', which is 一切; めったに would only mean 'rarely'.

jp: 事故[じこ]について、会社[かいしゃ]は責任[せきにん]を{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}負[お]いません。
en: The company accepts no responsibility at all for the accident.
why: Denying responsibility totally is 一切 + negative.

jp: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]の質問[しつもん]に{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}答[こた]えなかった。
en: He did not answer my questions at all.
why: Not a single answer was given: 一切 + negative means 'at all'.

jp: この店[みせ]は添加物[てんかぶつ]を{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}使[つか]っていません。
en: This shop uses no additives whatsoever.
why: 'None whatsoever' is 一切 + negative; めったに would admit occasional use.

jp: あの日[ひ]以来[いらい]、彼[かれ]からは{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}連絡[れんらく]がない。
en: Since that day I've had no contact from him at all.
why: Complete absence of contact is 一切 + ない.

jp: 私[わたし]はギャンブルを一切[いっさい]{しない|av-mettani}。
en: I don't gamble at all.
why: 一切 demands a negative predicate, so only しない fits.

jp: あの人[ひと]の話[はなし]は一切[いっさい]{信[しん]じられません|av-mettani}。
en: I can't believe anything that person says.
why: 一切 must be followed by a negative form such as 信じられません.

jp: 彼[かれ]はそのことを{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}知[し]らないと言[い]っている。
en: He says he knows nothing at all about it.
why: 'Nothing at all' is 一切 + 知らない.

jp: 今月[こんげつ]は{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}無駄遣[むだづか]いをしないと決[き]めた。
en: I decided not to waste any money at all this month.
why: A firm resolution of zero waste is 一切 + ない.

jp: この話[はなし]は社外[しゃがい]の人[ひと]には{一切[いっさい]|av-mettani}話[はな]さないでください。
en: Please don't tell anyone outside the company about this at all.
why: A strict prohibition 'not at all' takes 一切 before ないでください.
